title: Ezekiel 1:1–14
context: Ezekiel opens with a dated report. In 1:1 the prophet speaks in the first person: in the thirtieth year, among the captives by the river Chebar, “the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.” Verses 2–3 shift to a narrator’s voice, dating the word to “the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity” (conversions to a modern calendar are discussed rather than settled) and naming “Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi” in the land of the Chaldeans. What “the thirtieth year” counts from is not stated; a common proposal is the prophet’s age, and other reckonings have been suggested. The Chebar is often taken to be a canal in Babylonia, but its exact course is uncertain. From 1:4 the prophet describes a stormy wind from the north, a great cloud with fire and glowing metal, and four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings, moving straight forward wherever the spirit went. The description is careful and layered, with a repeated “likeness” and “appearance” and the hedge “as it were”, and this page follows that restraint. Ezekiel 10 later calls the creatures cherubim (compare 10:15 and 10:20), and Revelation 4:7 describes living creatures with comparable faces; those links are noted only in passing. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: the LORD reveals his glory to an exile far from the temple.

verses.text: Now in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet dates his vision and locates it “among the captives by the river Chebar”. Arminian readers note that the heavens open for an exile, far from Jerusalem and the temple. The LORD takes the initiative to meet his people where judgment has carried them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s free initiative: “the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as grace in exile, and both leave open what “the thirtieth year” counts from, since the text does not explain it.

verses.text: In the fifth of the month, which was the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity,
verses.arminianNotes: The date is tied to “the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity”. Arminian readers note how the book anchors revelation in real history. The exiles’ calendar is measured by their king’s captivity, a reminder of the covenant judgment they are living through.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise value the historical anchoring of the vision, often placed around 593 BC. Shared ground: both traditions read the dating as a sign that the LORD’s word enters concrete time, and both note that Jerusalem still stands at this point in the book.

verses.text: the LORD’s word came to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar; and the LORD’s hand was there on him.
verses.arminianNotes: A narrator names the recipient: “Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi”. Arminian readers note that “the LORD’s hand was there on him”, a phrase that recurs in the book (compare 3:14 and 3:22). The prophet’s experience is ascribed to the LORD’s initiative.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress the LORD’s hand as the sovereign source of the prophet’s call. Shared ground: both traditions see a priest in exile, far from temple service, drawn into a different service, and both read the verse as divine commissioning rather than personal ambition.

verses.text: I looked, and behold, a stormy wind came out of the north: a great cloud, with flashing lightning, and a brightness around it, and out of the middle of it as it were glowing metal, out of the middle of the fire.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet sees “a stormy wind came out of the north”, a great cloud, flashing lightning, brightness, and something “as it were glowing metal” in the fire. Arminian readers note storm imagery familiar from other appearances of the LORD (compare Exodus 19:16 and Psalm 18:9–12).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a theophany, the holy God approaching in fire and cloud. Shared ground: both traditions note that the prophet hedges his description (“as it were”), and both treat the north as a detail the text does not explain, so neither builds doctrine on it.

verses.text: Out of its center came the likeness of four living creatures. This was their appearance: They had the likeness of a man.
verses.arminianNotes: Out of the fire comes “the likeness of four living creatures”, and “They had the likeness of a man.” Arminian readers note the careful language. The prophet describes what he saw by comparison, not by exact definition, and readers are wise to keep the same restraint.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress the repeated “likeness” and the limits of human speech before God’s glory. Shared ground: both traditions read the creatures as heavenly attendants in the LORD’s presence, and both treat their later naming as cherubim (compare 10:20) as a link the book itself makes later.

verses.text: Everyone had four faces, and each one of them had four wings.
verses.arminianNotes: Each creature has four faces and four wings. Arminian readers usually resist decoding each feature. The symmetry may suggest completeness and readiness to move in every direction, though the text itself does not interpret the details.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise caution against overreading the imagery, while noting that the vision conveys majesty beyond ordinary categories. Shared ground: both traditions read the faces and wings as part of one overwhelming scene, not as a code to be solved verse by verse.

verses.text: Their feet were straight feet. The sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot; and they sparkled like burnished bronze.
verses.arminianNotes: Their feet were straight, with soles like a calf’s foot, and “they sparkled like burnished bronze.” Arminian readers note the gleaming, unearthly quality of the scene. The prophet stacks comparisons because ordinary words do not reach far enough.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see brilliance and stability in the description, fitting creatures who serve in God’s presence. Shared ground: both traditions read the details as descriptive rather than allegorical, and both let the prophet’s comparisons stand without supplying hidden meanings.

verses.text: They had the hands of a man under their wings on their four sides. The four of them had their faces and their wings like this:
verses.arminianNotes: They had “the hands of a man under their wings on their four sides.” Arminian readers note that the creatures are fitted for action as well as flight. Later in the book, a hand from among the cherubim plays a part in judgment on Jerusalem (compare 10:7–8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the creatures are servants ready to carry out the LORD’s purposes. Shared ground: both traditions read the hands as part of the vision’s description, connected to their later role in chapter 10, without building a doctrine on the detail itself.

verses.text: Their wings were joined to one another. They didn’t turn when they went. Each one went straight forward.
verses.arminianNotes: Their wings were joined, and “They didn’t turn when they went.” Arminian readers note the unity and directness of the creatures’ movement. They act together and without hesitation, a picture of service fully aligned with the purpose that moves them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the creatures moving in perfect concert with the will that directs them (compare 1:12). Shared ground: both traditions read the unturning motion as a picture of wholehearted, undivided service in the LORD’s presence.

verses.text: As for the likeness of their faces, they had the face of a man. The four of them had the face of a lion on the right side. The four of them had the face of an ox on the left side. The four of them also had the face of an eagle.
verses.arminianNotes: The four faces are those of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle. Arminian readers note that later Christian tradition attached various symbols to these faces, but the text itself does not interpret them, and they are best left as part of the vision’s grandeur.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the faces as part of the vision’s grandeur and leave the details uninterpreted where the text is silent. Shared ground: both traditions note the comparable faces in Revelation 4:7 only in passing and do not press a single identification.

verses.text: Such were their faces. Their wings were spread out above. Two wings of each one touched another, and two covered their bodies.
verses.arminianNotes: “Their wings were spread out above.” Two wings of each touched another, and two covered their bodies. Arminian readers note the posture of reverence alongside readiness. Even the creatures nearest the glory are covered, a hint of how holy the presence is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see reverent service, and some compare the covering wings of the seraphim in Isaiah 6:2, while noting that the descriptions differ. Shared ground: both traditions read the covering as an expression of holiness and awe, not as a detail to be pressed further.

verses.text: Each one went straight forward. Where the spirit was to go, they went. They didn’t turn when they went.
verses.arminianNotes: “Where the spirit was to go, they went.” Arminian readers note that the Hebrew word behind “spirit” can also mean wind or breath, so readers differ on how far to press it here. Either way, the creatures move by a directing will beyond themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the creatures’ movement governed entirely by the spirit that directs them, and some hear an anticipation of the Spirit who later lifts the prophet (compare 2:2 and 3:12). Shared ground: both read the verse as obedient motion and leave that link open.

verses.text: As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of torches. The fire went up and down among the living creatures. The fire was bright, and lightning went out of the fire.
verses.arminianNotes: Their appearance was “like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of torches”, with fire moving among them and lightning going out. Arminian readers note the fire as a sign of holiness and power. Later, coals from between the cherubim serve in judgment on the city (compare 10:2).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see holiness and judgment in the fire, linked with the coals scattered over Jerusalem in 10:2. Shared ground: both traditions read the fire as the danger and purity of the LORD’s presence, and both keep the link to chapter 10 in view without merging the two scenes.

verses.text: The living creatures ran and returned as the appearance of a flash of lightning.
verses.arminianNotes: “The living creatures ran and returned as the appearance of a flash of lightning.” Arminian readers note the speed and energy of the vision. The scene is not static; the heavenly attendants are alive and active in the service of the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see swiftness and readiness, fitting servants who do the will of the one enthroned above them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing the first part of the vision, before the prophet turns to the wheels in 1:15.
